g.text: Causal opacity refers to the difficulty in understanding a model's
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=1) Causal opacity refers to the difficulty in understanding a model's decision-making mechanisms (Termine & Primiero, 2024).

g.text: Like causal discovery, causal opacity, can be assessed through Pearl's
framework of causality (Pearl, 1995), categorizing an agent's causal
understanding based on its ability to answer three types of questions:
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=1) Like causal discovery, causal opacity, can be assessed through Pearl's framework of causality (Pearl, 1995), categorizing an agent's causal understanding based on its ability to answer three types of questions: observational queries ("what is the relationship between the feature x and the model's output?"), interventional queries ("what happens if I fix the feature x to a value k?"), and counterfactual queries ("what would the model's prediction had been if feature x had taken value k′ instead of k?").

g.text: Opacity = DNN decision process, not real-world
Unlike causal discovery, causal opacity concerns the decision-making process
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=0) Unlike causal discovery, causal opacity concerns the decision-making process of a DNN model.

g.text: Whether a DNN is causally opaque (or transparent) depends on whether users
can answer interventional and counterfactual questions that concern the
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=0) Whether a DNN is causally opaque (or transparent) depends on whether users can answer interventional and counterfactual questions that concern the model's inferential behaviour.

g.text: Opacity ≠ causal discovery; no true-DGP needed
In this regard, notice that (i) the problem of causal opacity is distinct
from the problem of causal discovery, which involves detecting causal
mechanisms in the real world, rather than understanding the causal structure
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=0) In this regard, notice that (i) the problem of causal opacity is distinct from the problem of causal discovery, which involves detecting causal mechanisms in the real world, rather than understanding the causal structure of a model's internal reasoning; and (ii) causal opacity (and the related form of causal understanding) neither implies nor requires discovering the "true" causal structure of the data-generating process.

g.text: Worked example: smoking ← lung cancer rule
For example, a model might effectively predict heart attacks based on the
rule heart_attack ← smoking ← lung_cancer, even though the actual biological
mechanism is that smoking causes lung cancer, not the reverse.
g.title: N6 [Context] (cites=0) For example, a model might effectively predict heart attacks based on the rule heart_attack ← smoking ← lung_cancer, even though the actual biological mechanism is that smoking causes lung cancer, not the reverse.

g.text: DL models are causally opaque on images
Deep Learning (DL) models (Fig. 1a) are causally opaque when
applied to unstructured data like images, as interventions on
low-level features, such as pixels, are not meaningful (Rudin,
2019; Ghorbani et al., 2019) and therefore do not…
g.title: N7 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Deep Learning (DL) models (Fig. 1a) are causally opaque when applied to unstructured data like images, as interventions on low-level features, such as pixels, are not meaningful (Rudin, 2019; Ghorbani et al., 2019) and therefore do not enable us to easily answer any of these sorts of questions.

g.text: For example, asking "what happens if I fix the intensity of the
pixel xi to k?" does little to reveal whether a DNN is exploiting
protected attributes like "gender" or "race" when classifying an
image of a person as a "doctor".
g.title: N8 [Limitation] (cites=0) For example, asking "what happens if I fix the intensity of the pixel xi to k?" does little to reveal whether a DNN is exploiting protected attributes like "gender" or "race" when classifying an image of a person as a "doctor".

g.text: Yet, understanding when these sorts of high-level attributes are
misused to make predictions is crucial for the proper verification
and vetting of models (Kusner et al., 2017), particularly in
g.title: N9 [Context] (cites=1) Yet, understanding when these sorts of high-level attributes are misused to make predictions is crucial for the proper verification and vetting of models (Kusner et al., 2017), particularly in high-impact real-world tasks (e.g., medical admission recommendations).

g.text: To address this issue, Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) (Koh et
al., 2020) have been designed to support interventions on
high-level interpretable features known as "concepts" (Kim et al.,
g.title: N10 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) To address this issue, Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) (Koh et al., 2020) have been designed to support interventions on high-level interpretable features known as "concepts" (Kim et al., 2018).

g.text: These concepts, whose semantics are aligned with units of information
experts would use to solve the same task, allow for more intuitive
interventions and counterfactual analysis (Wachter et al., 2017; Abid et
g.title: N11 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) These concepts, whose semantics are aligned with units of information experts would use to solve the same task, allow for more intuitive interventions and counterfactual analysis (Wachter et al., 2017; Abid et al., 2021).

g.text: This is because CBMs shift from reasoning based on raw features to
explicitly operating on interpretable variables such as "age", "income",
g.title: N12 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) This is because CBMs shift from reasoning based on raw features to explicitly operating on interpretable variables such as "age", "income", "gender", or "BMI".

g.text: CBMs rely on two unrealistic assumptions
Although CBMs are semantically transparent (Kim et al., 2018;
Facchini & Termine, 2021), we argue they still rely on two
g.title: N13 [Limitation] (cites=2) Although CBMs are semantically transparent (Kim et al., 2018; Facchini & Termine, 2021), we argue they still rely on two unrealistic assumptions (visualised in Fig. 1b).

g.text: First, they assume that concepts are causally independent, an
assumption that breaks in most real-world tasks. For instance,
CBMs might treat "smoking" and other health conditions as
independent predictors of an insurance premium, ignoring…
g.title: N13a [Limitation] (cites=0) First, they assume that concepts are causally independent, an assumption that breaks in most real-world tasks. For instance, CBMs might treat "smoking" and other health conditions as independent predictors of an insurance premium, ignoring how intervening on smoking affects health.

g.text: Second, and more importantly, CBMs assume concepts are the direct
g.title: N13b [Limitation] (cites=0) Second, and more importantly, CBMs assume concepts are the direct causes of model predictions.

g.text: These assumptions oversimplify and constrain the model's inference
structure, preventing the model from using more complex and effective
g.title: N14 [Limitation] (cites=1) These assumptions oversimplify and constrain the model's inference structure, preventing the model from using more complex and effective concept dependencies (Beckers, 2022).

g.text: As a result, the problem of causal opacity still represents a key open
challenge at the intersection of DL, causality, and XAI.
g.title: N15 [Limitation] (cites=0) As a result, the problem of causal opacity still represents a key open challenge at the intersection of DL, causality, and XAI.

g.text: In response to this challenge, we introduce Causal Concept Graph Models
g.title: N16 [Method] (cites=0) In response to this challenge, we introduce Causal Concept Graph Models (Causal CGMs, see Figure 1c).

g.text: Causal CGMs are a new concept-based architecture whose decision-making
process is causally transparent by design, avoiding the unrealistic
assumption that concepts must be causally independent and direct causes of
g.title: N17 [Method] (cites=0) Causal CGMs are a new concept-based architecture whose decision-making process is causally transparent by design, avoiding the unrealistic assumption that concepts must be causally independent and direct causes of class prediction.

g.text: The results of our experiments show that Causal CGMs can:
g.title: N18 [Contribution] (cites=0) The results of our experiments show that Causal CGMs can:

g.text: (i) match the generalisation performance of state-of-the-art
g.title: N18a [Contribution] (cites=0) (i) match the generalisation performance of state-of-the-art causally-opaque models,

g.text: C2: HITL corrections boost both accuracy + explanation
intermediate reasoning steps, boosting both downstream accuracy
g.title: N18b [Contribution] (cites=0) (ii) enable human-in-the-loop corrections of mispredicted intermediate reasoning steps, boosting both downstream accuracy and explanation correctness,

g.text: and (iii) support the analysis of both interventional and
counterfactual questions, improving causal interpretability and
enabling effective verification of reliability and fairness.
g.title: N18c [Contribution] (cites=0) and (iii) support the analysis of both interventional and counterfactual questions, improving causal interpretability and enabling effective verification of reliability and fairness.
